title: Sex‐specific cumulative effects of inbreeding on lifetime fitness in purple‐crowned fairy‐wrens
content:
Using unusually accurate fitness measures and genomic inbreeding estimates, this research assesses the effect of inbreeding on fitness across the lifetime of individual purple-crowned fairy-wrens. The findings of large inbreeding effects on lifetime fitness emphasise that inbreeding depression in wild populations may be underestimated if the lifetime impacts of inbreeding cannot be quantified.


Abstract

Complex environmental and genetic factors can cause inbreeding depression to vary across different life-history stages. However, disentangling inbreeding effects over the full lifespan remains challenging, as the required combination of detailed genomic, individual and ecological information is rarely available in natural populations. Here, we assess the effect of genomic inbreeding on fitness in the purple-crowned fairy-wren (Malurus coronatus coronatus), an endangered tropical passerine. Our study population has unusually accurate lifetime fitness measures for both sexes acquired during two decades of intensive individual-based study. We found evidence of more frequent inbreeding in the population than we would expect, given behavioural inbreeding avoidance. There was no evidence for a relationship between inbreeding and survival in the first year of life, despite our large sample size and ability to control for known environmental factors important in early-life. However, we found a negative relationship between inbreeding and the probability of breeding position acquisition as well as lifespan, resulting in substantially reduced lifetime fitness. Structural equation models identified an additional direct negative effect of inbreeding on lifetime reproductive success that was present in males only, despite very similar investment in offspring care by both parents. Overall, our results suggest pervasive, late-acting or cumulative effects of inbreeding that are partly sex-specific. Our findings emphasise that inbreeding depression in wild populations may be underestimated if cumulative lifetime impacts of inbreeding cannot be quantified. Additional study of inbreeding load and environmental interactions would be valuable in further understanding the mechanisms of inbreeding depression and the genomic and ecological factors underlying the sex difference. This is particularly important given the large reduction in lifetime fitness associated with realised levels of inbreeding in this population and the ongoing anthropogenic threats it is facing.
